To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ectocervix cells (ECE) retain a high level of differentiation in culture and express in vivo-like cytokeratins (K13, K14 and K15).
ectocervix epithelial cells (EC) retain a high level of differentiated function when grown in culture using feeder layers.

human ectocervix epithelial cells cultured on feeder layers retain a high degree (80% or greater) of differentiated function, as demonstrated by the expression of cytokeratin markers and the responsiveness to sex steroid regulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the ectocervical (endocervical) epithelium in the female reproductive process.
the maintenance and expression of the differentiated phenotype of ectocervical and endocervical epithelia.
the study of human cervical epithelial cells in culture and the regulation of the differentiation of this epithelium by steroid hormones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ECE cells are a good in vitro model of the normal ectocervix.
the ECE cell culture system is an excellent model for studying the biology of the ectocervical mucosa.
the in vitro culture system for ectocervical cell differentiation described in the present manuscript is a valuable tool for the study of normal ectocerical epithelial cell physiology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cultured ECE cell model system retains a high degree of normal in vivo-like differentiation.
ECE cells retain a high degree (greater than or equal to 80%) of in vivo-like cytokeratin expression, sex-steroid responsiveness and estrogen receptor (ER) expression in culture.
the cultured ECE cell system is an excellent model for the study not only of the regulation of ectocervical cell function but also the study of epithelial cell differentiation in general.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cultured ECE cell system provides an excellent model for the study and maintenance of in vivo-like ectocervical differentiation.
ECE cell culture provides a useful model for studying sex steroid regulation of ectocervical differentiation.
the ECE cells are a useful model for study of the normal ectocervix.
